Yesterday Kevin Kotecki and I had the chance to spend some time with Jensen Huang and the team at NVIDIA.

We’re grateful for the opportunity to share more of what we’ve been building at Tailscale—and where we think connectivity needs to go next.

A lot of the conversation centered around a shift that’s already underway: networks are no longer just connecting servers. They’re connecting AI systems, robotics, and hardware that was never designed to work together, from cutting-edge GPUs to older devices still doing critical work.

That creates a surprisingly hard problem.

How do you make all of that interoperable without rebuilding everything from scratch? How do you give AI systems and physical devices secure, identity-based access to each other, across environments, without adding layers of complexity that break the moment something changes?

Our view is that the network has to become simpler, not more complicated. More like a shared fabric that different systems can plug into, regardless of where they run or when they were built.

A lot of what we’re doing at Tailscale is aimed at exactly that: connecting AI infrastructure, bridging old and new hardware, and making it all work as one coherent system.

It was energizing to compare notes with a team thinking deeply about these problems from a completely different layer of the stack.

Looking forward to continuing the conversation.

A lot of security work starts as checkbox security.

This year, one of the most effective checkboxes seems to be cyber insurance. Not because insurers are security experts, but because they keep asking questions that are awkwardly hard to answer if your privileged access story is “uhhh… Dave has the admin password.”

Sometimes that deserves skepticism. But PAM is one of the rare checkboxes that points at a real problem.

A framing that seems to help is this: “I don’t actually want a user on the network. I want them to reach this service.” That mental shift removes a surprising number of headaches.

Privileged access is where accidents become incidents. Long-lived admin credentials, shared secrets, broad access “just in case.” Those shortcuts feel efficient right up until they aren’t.

What I worry about, especially for teams tackling PAM seriously for the first time, is that the default solution is often “buy a vault.” Put the powerful passwords somewhere safer, rotate them more often, add approvals, record sessions. Better than nothing, but also a lot of machinery to manage a thing that maybe shouldn’t exist in the first place.

The simpler model is: stop handing out standing privilege. Use identity. Use policy. Make access just-in-time, tightly scoped, and auditable. Then take that access away automatically.

This is where the network layer helps more than people expect. If access is tied to identity and enforced by ACLs, you do not need humans carrying secrets around at all. You decide who can talk to what, under which conditions, and you log it.

At Tailscale, people often arrive thinking about connectivity. They leave thinking about access. And once you start from identity plus policy, a bunch of “traditional PAM” complexity just stops being necessary.

Insurance and audits might be what gets people to look at PAM. The best outcome is not more vaults. It’s fewer privileges, fewer secrets, and less drama when something goes wrong.

We did not have “distributed systems in the Millennium Falcon” on our 2026 bingo card, but here we are.

Avery on why even toys are real networks now. 🧱

LEGO quietly shipped a self-organizing network made out of plastic bricks.

No hub. No app. No screen. Their new Smart Bricks (link in comments) discover each other over Bluetooth, share state, and coordinate behavior. LEGO calls it BrickNet, which is a charming name for “there’s a distributed system in your kid’s Millennium Falcon now.”

As a networking person, I love this.

It’s small, local, and purpose-built. The network exists only to make the toy work, then mostly disappears. No cloud account, no dashboard, no SaaS subscription for the left thruster. That’s actually a very sane design choice.

It’s also where the interesting questions start.

Bluetooth instead of Wi-Fi means a different trust model: proximity as authentication, pairing semantics nobody ever sees, keys that may outlive the play session they were meant for. “No setup” doesn’t mean no security decisions, it just means they were made for you, ahead of time.

None of this is a complaint. Quite the opposite. This is networking at a human scale: ephemeral, local, and mostly invisible. Honestly, it’s probably more robust than half the IoT gadgets people install in their homes.

Still, toys are real networks now, running real protocols, in the same rooms as everything else we care about. At some point two fleets of star destroyers meet, or someone figures out how to talk to the bricks in an unexpected way, and the boundary between “play” and “infrastructure” gets fuzzy.

If my kids' LEGO set starts advertising routes, I’m definitely asking where the ACLs live.

Fraudulent Candidates Are Everywhere—Here’s What We’re Doing About It

Over the last few months, we’ve seen a huge rise in fraudulent applicants here at Tailscale. In some cases, as many as half of applicants on a job are not who they say they are. Yes, really.

The good news: we’ve gotten very good at spotting it, and I wanted to share what I have learned.

🎯 Who’s a Target?
-remote-first tech companies
-companies with fully remote interview processes

❓ Why? Fraudsters are hoping they can:
-impersonate someone else
-use deepfake video or audio
-bypass less-rigorous screening steps
-eventually steal data or paychecks

Basically, anywhere the hiring process happens behind a laptop, fraud is rising. 

🛑 The Most Telltale Signs:
-no profile photo (or a cartoon avatar- as much as we love them!) on LinkedIn
-no connections or a brand-new LinkedIn account
-application language suspiciously close to the exact verbiage in your job description
-different name on the resume vs email vs LinkedIn
 (not just a nickname… literally different identities)
-repeated applications even after being rejected
-listing n/a in job posting questions to bypass or writing nonsensical answers

⚠️ Important:
One flag alone does not mean fraud—but multiple flags together should absolutely make you pause and verify.

Some Tips
👉 Message them on LinkedIn before the interview
If the LinkedIn looks legit but something else feels off, send a message and ask them to confirm the interview time.
If it’s a fraudulent applicant, 1 of 2 things might happen:
1) the real person responds (“um…who??”) 2) the scammer disappears
Either way, you get clarity without wasting time.
👉 Email before the interview. You can literally say: “We’ve been seeing a lot of fraudulent applications—would you mind confirming X?” Most legitimate candidates won’t mind at all.
👉 For Engineers, ask for a GitHub link in your application questions & have them to add you to a private repo (takes 30 seconds).
👉 Use verification tools. We use tofu, and it’s been excellent. It can tell you:
-if their email address or LinkedIn was created yesterday
-whether the email matches the LinkedIn signup
-if the phone number is tied to prior scams
-whether the same resume shows up under multiple names at your company or the countless others in their network

It’s worth the investment—especially if you’re remote and high-volume.

💡 Remember:
Behind every scam attempt, there’s sometimes a real person whose identity is being abused. If you confirm something is fraudulent, be kind and send a quick InMail to the person. Most have no idea someone applied on their behalf.

TL;DR
Fraudulent applicants are here, they’re getting more sophisticated, and we’re not tolerating it. At Tailscale, we’re actively verifying identity, tightening processes, and investing in tools. If you’re a hiring manager or recruiter dealing with the same, I hope this helps. And if you’re a scammer thinking of applying here… please don’t. We’re onto you. 😉

I’ve been thinking a lot about the “edge” lately. Not the buzzwordy one in slide decks, but the real edge: the scruffy little embedded devices running the world while nobody’s looking.

Forbes just published a piece I wrote (link in comments) about exactly that: why the most critical infrastructure in 2025 isn’t running in the cloud, or on a desktop OS, or even patched on any predictable schedule, it’s running quietly, out of sight, on tiny computers that rarely get updated and never get the attention they deserve.

What makes this fun is seeing how companies are actually solving these problems today.

Two great examples:
Dexory is out there running entire fleets of autonomous warehouse robots, where “just reboot it” is not a plan and the network has to work even when everything around it is noisy, dusty, or generally behaving like a warehouse does on its busiest day. 

Meanwhile, DEEL Media is managing thousands of digital displays scattered across retail environments where nobody has time, or the desire, to SSH into anything ever again. Both of them are great examples of what we keep seeing at the edge: real companies solving real problems on devices that quietly run the world.

And they’re not alone. Every week we hear from more teams, big enterprises, small startups, and a surprising number of folks who deploy Raspberry Pis into places Raspberry Pis were never meant to go (Andrew McCalip, I'm looking at you!) all using Tailscale to make edge connectivity simple, secure, and boring in the best possible way.

The pattern is the same everywhere: you can’t rely on perfect firmware, perfect networks, or perfect device management. So you design systems that stay safe even when nothing else is perfect.

Because the truth is simple: the world doesn’t run on macOS or Windows on high-end laptops. It runs on Linux on robots, kiosks, factory sensors, and a million tiny embedded devices nobody ever remembers to update.

If we secure that world properly, everything else gets a lot better too.

- Malicious MCP / Tool Use
- Poor Server Configuration / Implementation
- Sandbox Escapes  
- Credential Theft or Reuse
- Supply Chain Compromises
- Protocol Issues / Attacks

While this might not scare off someone using an LLM with web browsing to research vacations destinations, it definitely gives IT & Security a real reason to worry.

I read a post in Wired this week about how some corners of the tech industry are embracing the controversial 996 work schedule — 9am to 9pm, six days a week. (Link in comments.)

It reminded me of something we’ve all seen before.

Back in the early 2000s, the story was outsourcing.
“Developers overseas will replace your whole team for a tenth the cost.”
At the same time:
“Can your team move faster? We’re falling behind. Maybe they just don’t want it enough.”

Now, we’ve replaced “outsourcing” with “AI.”
“LLMs will write the code, do the tests, fix the bugs.”
Also:
“By the way, we need you to commit to a 996 schedule. 72 hours a week. You’re either all-in, or you’re out.”

We’re told that human work is replaceable — but also, we need to give more of ourselves. Just in case.

I don’t believe in that framing. The contradiction is exhausting.

Good work takes time. It takes energy and space.
Teams that are well-rested build better systems. They make better decisions. They support each other through the messy parts — and they don’t burn out after sprint three.

You can love your work. A lot of us do. But your work can't love you back. It won't protect your weekends. It won't tell you to close the laptop and go for a walk.

That’s our job. As leaders, as teammates.

The goal isn’t just to build great products. It’s to build them in a way that’s sustainable, respectful, and — ideally — kind.

And if that sounds slow? It’s probably faster in the long run.

You’ve probably seen the story: a UK logistics company, Knights of Old, was taken offline by a single bad password. https://lnkd.in/gi47iuNA

First — let's have some empathy. Nobody wants to be that company. And yet, even in 2025, this keeps happening. We’ve spent years telling people to use strong, unique passwords. But here’s the uncomfortable truth: even if you do everything right with passwords, it still might not be enough.

That’s because a password (or a login link, or a YubiKey, or Face ID...) only handles authentication. It answers the question: Are you who you say you are?

But the more important question is: Now that you're in, what are you allowed to do? That’s authorization. And most networks don’t separate those two concerns very well.

At Tailscale, we don’t manage your credentials — we delegate authentication to providers like Google, Microsoft, Okta, Apple, etc. But that’s just step one.

Step two is defining policy: who can access what, from where, when, and how. We use Grants and ACLs (access control lists) and service-level rules to make sure that even if a password leaks, the attacker doesn't get the whole network. They get only what the legitimate user was authorized to access — which might be a dev sandbox and not, say, production systems.

Think of it like this: authentication gives you the front door key. Authorization decides whether that key opens just the guest bathroom or the vault in the basement.

Layer on an MDM service like Jamf or Kandji, , and suddenly even access to the guest bathroom requires you to be wearing long pants instead of shorts. Because security is about posture (and pants), not just presence. ;) 

Passwords still matter. But policies matter more. If you haven’t updated your authorization model in a while, don’t wait for a ransomware headline to remind you.

Everyone thinks “simple” is easy. In reality, it’s one of the hardest things to do — especially over time.

Take Tailscale. We had one platform when we launched in 2019. We still have one in 2025. And, if we do our jobs right, we’ll still have one in 2030.

That’s not because we’ve been sitting still. Last year I quote-skeeted someone on Bluesky who said they could build Tailscale in a weekend. My reply: “Sure. And we’ve been debugging it ever since.”
https://lnkd.in/gAEt9NMf

It was a joke, but it’s also kind of the whole point. It’s easy to ship something once. It’s hard to keep refining it, improving it, simplifying it — especially when everything around you pushes toward adding more.

Most companies in our space start with one product. Then they add a second. Then a third. Eventually they have a “suite.” That’s a valid strategy, and sometimes it works well. But somewhere along the way, the clarity of the original idea gets blurry.

For me, and for us at Tailscale, simplicity isn’t a constraint — it’s the mission. Making networks just work, without configuration files or VPN gateways or “quickstart” guides longer than your arm.

I wrote a whole blog post last year about this vision for a new kind of Internet:
https://lnkd.in/gdzMR-AC

It’s not about nostalgia (but yes, it was a reference to the show Silicon Valley that kind of took on a life of its own!) It’s about how things should work. Direct, secure, peer-to-peer. The kind of simplicity that’s invisible because it’s doing its job.

And yes, we’re a business. If we keep doing this well, we’ll make money. But the focus — on simplicity, usability, and delight — is what keeps me going every day.

So I’m curious:
What’s your version of simplicity?
What’s the thing you’ve resisted overbuilding, sometimes at great cost, because it mattered more to keep it clear?

I’d love to hear your stories.
